title: Light-induced effective magnetic fields in Landau quantized graphene
authors: Hiroki Ueda, Alexej Pashkin, Ece Uykur, Kryštof Kašša, Filip Chudoba, Jan Kunc, Manfred Helm, Milan Orlita, Stephan Winnerl
abstract: Ultrafast magnetism triggered by circularly polarized radiation underpins ultrafast spin control, relevant to future technologies, e.g., opto-spintronics and magnonics. The dynamics are often complicated and intertwined among correlated subsystems, such as electrons, spins, phonons, plasmons, topology, and lattice, due to many-body quantum coupling at ultrafast timescales. Here, we demonstrate light-induced effective magnetic fields generated by selective excitation between non-equidistant Landau quantized states in graphene, a prototypical Dirac material, using circularly polarized pulses. By magnetically tuning the Landau-level transition resonance away from other low-energy excitations, we obtain a clean electrostatically controllable platform and identify the microscopic origin of the light-induced magnetic signals, independent of sublattice coupling. Because different Landau levels carry distinct optical Hall conductivities, direct modification of their occupancies via optical excitations creates transient Faraday rotation signals with dispersive magnetic-field dependence, mirroring the static magneto-optical lineshape. The induced effective magnetic field normalized by the pump electric field exceeds typical reported values for the inverse Faraday effect of electronic origin. Our results establish a clear microscopic picture of the inverse Faraday effect of electronic origin, which can trigger hierarchical dynamics among correlated sublattices once Landau-level transitions are magnetically tuned to coincide with other low-energy excitations in Dirac systems and related materials.
summary: This paper experimentally demonstrates how circularly polarized light can induce transient effective magnetic fields in graphene by selectively exciting transitions between Landau quantized energy levels. By analyzing the resulting magneto-optical response, the authors establish a clear microscopic picture of the electronic inverse Faraday effect, opening avenues for ultrafast control over spin and magnetoelectric functionalities.
main_problem: Investigating light-induced effective magnetic fields generated by circularly polarized radiation in graphene, relevant for ultrafast spin control.
main_result: The study demonstrates a direct, time-resolved link between resonant Landau-level excitation and the modification of optical Hall conductivity, generating an effective magnetic field on the order of 10 mT.
method: Time-resolved pump-probe spectroscopy using circularly polarized terahertz pulses ($\sigma^+$ and $\sigma^-$) to selectively excite non-equidistant Landau quantized states in graphene.
model_or_system: The physical system is graphene, a prototypical Dirac material, studied under an applied magnetic field ($B$) where electron energy levels are quantized into Landau levels. The analysis focuses on the electronic origin of the inverse Faraday effect.
key_observables: Transient Faraday rotation signals ($\Delta	heta$), differential transmission ($\Delta T/T$), and the extracted effective magnetic field ($\mathbf{B}_{	ext{eff}}$).
important_parameters: Pump fluence ($\sim 1.6 \mu	ext{J}/	ext{cm}^2$); Effective magnetic field magnitude ($\sim 10 	ext{ mT}$); Landau level transitions ($n=-1 	o n=0$, etc.).
main_assumptions: The fast-timescale dynamics are attributed purely to electronic effects via the optical Hall conductivity, isolating this mechanism from phonon or sublattice contributions.
figures_summary: Figures show energy diagrams of Landau levels and time traces of polarization rotation ($\Delta	heta$) vs. delay time at various magnetic fields, demonstrating field dependence across resonance.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical problem (ultrafast spin control), details the experimental setup using selective resonant excitation in graphene's Landau levels, analyzes the magneto-optical response by separating contributions ($\Delta	heta_F$), and concludes that the signal originates from the optical Hall conductivity mechanism.
why_interesting: The work provides a clean, tunable platform to observe fundamental many-body quantum coupling effects (like the inverse Faraday effect) in Dirac materials using light, which is highly relevant for developing next-generation opto-spintronic devices.
